children: The average price of a gallon of diesel in the U.S. hit a fresh record high of $6.27 on Tuesday, according to the American Automobile Association.

U.S. diesel prices are soaring once again as the squeeze in the fuel market tightens, breaching $6 a gallon for the first time on Friday. Higher prices at the pump come as Brent Crude trades at around $107 a barrel, with renewed supply concerns mounting and Northern Hemisphere farmers entering the diesel-intensive harvesting season.
Prices had jumped at the start of the Iran conflict before cooling after refiners ramped up production. The average price for a gallon of diesel was $3.69 a year ago.

The higher prices are a blow to President Trump who made easing the cost of living central to his 2024 re-election campaign and has repeatedly called for lower interest rates. However, energy-cost inflation has boosted expectations that the U.S. Federal Reserve will hike interest rates Wednesday.
In California, the average price of diesel was at $8.21 a gallon, the AAA said Tuesday.

The U.S. 3-2-1 crack spread--a widely watched industry benchmark that measures the value of turning three barrels of crude oil into two barrels of gasoline and one barrel of diesel--sits at $62.62. It is typically in the teens. The high margin shows demand for refined products is outpacing refiners ability to produce and that each barrel of refined product is considerably more valuable than the crude used to make it.
Diesel prices are set to remain high as the winter heating season approaches and demand for heating fuels grows.

Supplies could fall just as demand ticks up, with refineries expected to undergo seasonal maintenance over the coming months. Refiners have been running their plants hard throughout the conflict to capture the extraordinary margins and have delayed any nonessential work during this time, compounding the maintenance backlog.

The Trump administration has tried to increase the country's fuel-making capacity while rejecting persistent speculation that it is seriously weighing a temporary ban on U.S. exports of refined products such as diesel.

Any ban could offer some immediate relief but would eventually weigh on refinery margins and lead to refiners cutting run rates, ING analysts said in a note. The loss of supply would mean higher prices over the longer-term.

The fuel market has become considerably tighter as the war in the Middle East progresses. Easy-to-access oil that was stored on ocean tankers is being used while strategic reserves in the U.S. and around the world are drawn down.

Hopes that increasing oil flows coming out of the Middle East would help alleviate some of the pressure were dented after an attack last week on a crucial crude pipeline in Saudi Arabia that helped bypass the Strait of Hormuz, a key chokepoint for oil exports that was hit by the conflict. This has stranded at least 2.5 million barrels a day, analysts estimate.
A Russian ban on diesel exports following Ukrainian drone attacks on its refineries has added to the lost volumes.

Diesel is a key part of the global economy, fueling trucks that move food and manufactured goods, heavy equipment at construction sites and ships at sea. It is also widely used for heating. A prolonged supply crunch can ripple through the economy, pushing up freight rates and the cost of food, construction and household fuel.
